title: Intention-to-Treat Error
hook: The people who leave the trial may be the people telling you whether it worked.
counterintuition: A cleaner success rate can be less honest; keep people in their assigned groups before the dropouts make the result look better than it is.
keyTakeaway: Intention-to-treat protects the original comparison. Count people by assigned group, including switchers and dropouts, before deciding what worked.

breakdown.fastRead: The wildfire planning room celebrates a fuel-saving route because the crews that finished the test used less fuel. Carolyn points to the fuel receipt pile and asks about crews assigned to the route who abandoned it during smoke, detours, or equipment trouble. The result changes. Intention-to-treat error appears when you judge only the people who stuck with the plan. The people who leave the trial may be the people telling you whether it worked.
breakdown.deepRead:
A clean result often comes from cleaning away the difficult people. The patients who stopped taking the drug, the users who left the beta, the crews who abandoned the route, the investors who moved their money, and the students who missed sessions all make the table untidy. Removing them can make the treatment, feature, route, fund, or program look stronger.

Intention-to-treat keeps the comparison honest by counting people in the groups they were assigned to at the start. If a clinical trial assigns one group to a treatment and another to a control, the result should not quietly erase the people who quit because of side effects, confusion, cost, or lack of benefit. Those exits are not administrative noise. They are part of what the treatment does in the world.

Dropouts are evidence with their coats on.

The correction is to protect the assignment before reading the outcome. Ask who was assigned, who switched, who dropped out, and whether the headline result counts all of them. Then decide from the assigned groups, not from the tidiest survivors.

A software beta shows the move. Jeffrey sees a dashboard where active users love the prototype. Before green-lighting the feature, he marks assigned groups on the prototype log and adds the users who were invited but never activated, the users who quit after two sessions, and the users who switched back to the old flow. He is not punishing the feature. He is keeping the comparison from being edited by endurance.
breakdown.fullRead:
The biotech signal review starts with a flattering chart. Lillian sees a control chart where the patients who completed all visits improved more than the control group. The room wants to call the signal promising. Then she asks for the assigned groups: everyone offered the treatment, everyone assigned to control, the patients who dropped because of nausea, the patients who missed visits, and the ones who crossed over to another therapy.

The intention-to-treat principle exists because compliance is not neutral. People do not drop out at random. They quit because the treatment hurts, disappoints, costs too much, confuses them, or fails to fit their life. If you count only the finishers, you may be measuring the treatment plus the special qualities of people able to finish it. The assigned group is the anchor that keeps the comparison from drifting.

Who disappeared from the success rate?

Statistical Considerations in the Intent-to-Treat Principle, associated with Lachin's work on clinical trials, puts pressure on this exact point: the analysis should preserve the randomized or assigned comparison as far as possible. That is not a technical courtesy. It is a guardrail against letting the result be rewritten after the hard cases leave.

A cycling crash audit makes the error visible outside medicine. You are looking at an exam sheet for riders assigned to a safety course. Regina, the city analyst, must decide whether the course reduced crashes. The simple report counts only riders who completed every session. She adds riders assigned to the course who skipped sessions after near misses, riders who changed routes, and riders who stopped cycling. The crash rate becomes less flattering and more useful.

The assigned group is the promise the evidence made before it knew the answer.

A touring theater budget shows the same pattern. Murray reviews a market memo saying the new subscription plan improved attendance among subscribers who stayed all season. The missing people are the ones assigned to the offer who canceled after the first show, failed to redeem tickets, or moved to single purchases. If the budget counts only loyal subscribers, the plan looks like magic. If it counts the assigned group, the plan looks like a tool with friction.

The practical correction is a small table. Column one: assigned to the option. Column two: completed as planned. Column three: switched or quit. Column four: outcome counted where? If the report jumps from assigned people to finishers without explaining the missing column, you are looking at a possible intention-to-treat error.

The limit is that no analysis can make missing data perfect. Some people vanish completely. Some switch for reasons nobody recorded. Some outcomes cannot be recovered. Still, the first honest question remains stable: what happened to everyone who was originally assigned? When the answer is unclear, lower your confidence. When the answer is visible, let the assigned groups carry the decision.

examples.title: Carolyn counts the crews that left
examples.scenario: The fuel receipt pile sits between smoke maps in a Kelowna wildfire planning room at 5:45 a.m. Carolyn, the logistics lead, must decide whether a new route saved fuel. She writes intention-to-treat on the receipts, adds crews assigned to the route who abandoned it, and changes the route recommendation.
examples.whatToDo: Count crews by original route assignment before judging fuel savings.
examples.whyItMatters: The finishers may have saved fuel because the difficult cases left the test. The abandoned assignments belong in the result.

examples.title: Cecile reopens the pension postmortem
examples.scenario: Which retirees vanished before the fund's advice program reported success? Cecile reviews the Montreal pension committee postmortem at 4:05 p.m. with a closed-door list beside the binders. She marks intention, adds members assigned to advice who opted out or changed funds, and changes the performance note.
examples.whatToDo: Track the advice program from assignment through opt-outs before judging performance.
examples.whyItMatters: The remaining participants may be unusually engaged. The people who left are part of the program's real effect.

reviewCards.front: A success rate counts only people who finished. Who must stay in the denominator?
reviewCards.back: Keep dropouts, switchers, and noncompliers in the assigned groups. Completion-only rates can flatter the intervention.

reviewCards.front: A trial result looks cleaner after dropouts disappear. What is the danger?
reviewCards.back: The missing people may be the evidence that the treatment was hard, harmful, confusing, or weak.

reviewCards.front: A beta dashboard shows active users love the feature. What comparison is missing?
reviewCards.back: Compare everyone assigned or invited to the beta, including people who never activated or quit early.

reviewCards.front: A program counts only loyal participants. What table should you ask for?
reviewCards.back: Ask for assigned, completed, switched or quit, and where each outcome was counted.

reviewCards.front: Some assigned people vanished completely. What should happen to confidence?
reviewCards.back: Lower confidence and make the missing assigned group visible instead of treating finishers as the whole effect.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Protect the original assigned groups before judging whether an option worked.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a result reports finishers, then I will ask for everyone originally assigned.
If active users look happy, then I will ask who was invited, who never activated, and who quit.
If completers improve, then I will compare assigned students or employees including missed sessions.
If loyal participants outperform, then I will include opt-outs, switchers, and silent members.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one result based on completers. Write the original assigned group, the dropouts, and where the missing outcomes were counted.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one program metric by drawing the path from assignment to completion, switch, dropout, and outcome.

tryThisNow: Choose one result that counts finishers. Write the original assigned group, then add the dropouts before trusting the success rate.
